title: Access and use information from texts

lessons.title: Finding information in work texts
lessons.html:
Texts are everywhere at work

A text is anything with words, numbers or pictures that gives you a message. At an abattoir, grain silo or poultry plant you see many texts every day:

  • Safety signs on walls and machines
  • Notices on the notice board, such as shift changes
  • Labels on cleaning chemicals
  • Work instructions and checklists
  • Payslips and leave forms
  • Delivery notes and weighbridge slips

Know why you are reading

Before you read, ask yourself: what do I need to find out? For example: 'What time does my shift start next week?' or 'How much water do I mix with this chemical?' This helps you look only for the part you need.

Skimming and scanning

  • Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea. Look at the heading, pictures and first lines.
  • Scanning means running your eyes over the text to find one fact, like a date, a name or a number.

Using headings and layout

Most work texts have headings, numbered steps, bold words and tables. Use these to find information fast. On a chemical label, for example, look for headings like 'Directions for use', 'Warning' and 'First aid'.

If a word is new to you, look at the words around it to guess the meaning, ask a co-worker or your supervisor, or use a dictionary. Never guess when it comes to safety or chemicals. Always ask.

lessons.title: Reading signs, symbols and pictures
lessons.html:
Messages without many words

Many important messages at work use colours, shapes and pictures instead of words. You must know what they mean, because they keep you safe.

Safety sign colours and shapes

SignMeaningExample
Red circle with a line through itDo not do thisNo smoking
Blue circleYou must do thisWear gloves, wear ear protection
Yellow triangleWarning, dangerSlippery floor, electricity
Green squareSafe conditionEmergency exit, first aid box
Red squareFire equipmentFire extinguisher, fire hose

Hazard pictures on chemical labels

Cleaning and sanitising chemicals have pictures in a red diamond. These show if a product can burn your skin, is poisonous, can catch fire or harms the environment. If you see these, wear the correct protective clothing and follow the label.

Pictures in work instructions

Some instructions use drawings to show steps, such as how to wash your hands before entering the production area or how to put on a hairnet and boots. Follow the pictures in order.

Charts and graphs

Your team may have a chart on the wall showing, for example, how many birds were processed each day. Read the heading, then the labels on the sides, then look for the highest and lowest points.

If you do not understand a sign or symbol, ask your supervisor. Do not ignore it.

lessons.title: Using information to act
lessons.html:
Reading so that you can do something

We read at work so that we can act correctly. After reading, you should be able to follow the steps, fill in a form or tell someone what the text said.

Following written instructions

  1. Read all the steps first before you start.
  2. Get everything you need ready.
  3. Do each step in order. Tick it off if there is a checklist.
  4. If a step is unclear, stop and ask.
  5. When you finish, check the result.

Filling in forms

Forms such as a leave form or a cleaning checklist ask for information in boxes. Read each heading carefully. Write clearly in block letters if asked. Fill in the date, your name and your signature where needed. Check that the numbers are correct before you hand it in.

Fact or opinion

Some texts give facts, like 'The cold room must stay below a set temperature'. Others give opinions, like 'This is the best canteen in town'. At work, follow the facts in official procedures, not rumours or opinions.

Telling others what you read

Sometimes you must pass on a message from a notice to a co-worker who did not see it. Say the main point in your own words, with the important facts such as dates and times.

Key points

  • Know what you are looking for before you read.
  • Skim for the main idea and scan for a specific fact.
  • Learn safety sign colours and shapes: red no, blue must, yellow warning, green safe.
  • Read all steps before starting an instruction.
  • Ask when you do not understand, especially with chemicals and safety.
